title: Genesis 33:1–20

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Esau’s embrace, and Jacob’s altar to El-Elohe-Israel—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Genesis 33:1–20.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Eleven or twelve little ones followed Jacob, the eldest of them not fourteen years old: Who are these? saith Esau. Jacob had sent him an account of the increase of his estate, but made no mention of his children, perhaps because he would not expose them to his rage, if he should meet him as an enemy. Esau therefore had reason to ask who are those with thee?
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 33:5)

reformed.quote: We have said how greatly Jacob feared for himself from his brother; but now when Esau himself approaches, his terror is not only renewed, but increased. For although he goes forth like a courageous and spirited combatant to this contest, he is still not exempt from a sense of danger; whence it follows, that he is not free, either from anxiety or fear. For his cruel brother had still the same cause of hatred against him as before.

context: After Peniel, Jacob lifts his eyes and Esau comes with four hundred men. Jacob arranges his household, bows seven times, and finds not a sword but an embrace. Gifts are pressed and received; travel plans part them—Esau to Seir, Jacob to Succoth, then safely to Shechem in Canaan, where he buys land and raises an altar: El-Elohe-Israel.

verses.text: And Jacob lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, Esau was coming, and four hundred men with him. So he divided the children among Leah and Rachel and the two female servants.
verses.arminianNotes: The feared hour arrives: Esau with four hundred. Jacob still acts—dividing the children. Grace at the Jabbok did not erase responsible care; he meets the crisis with planning, not paralysis.
verses.reformedNotes: What Jacob dreaded in prayer (32:11) now stands on the road. The four hundred are real, yet they arrive under the God who already met Jacob in the night. Providence has not cancelled the meeting; it governs it.

verses.text: And he put the servants with their children in front, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph last of all.
verses.arminianNotes: The line is ranked by affection and risk. Love is real, and so is fear. Jacob’s ordering is a human, accountable choice—protecting the dearest last—not a picture of a man with no agency left.
verses.reformedNotes: Even the sequence of the camp sits inside a larger keeping. Rachel and Joseph last does not mean the promise hangs on Jacob’s tactics; the God of Peniel still holds the line that will run through Joseph.

verses.text: He himself went on before them, bowing himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob goes first and bows seven times. Humility toward the brother he wronged is a real moral step: grace enables repentance’s posture without forcing Esau’s response.
verses.reformedNotes: The supplanter walks ahead as a servant. Sevenfold bowing is not theater that buys safety; it is the fruit of a man God has already crippled and blessed. The Lord can humble a heel-grabber before a human brother.

verses.text: But Esau ran to meet him and embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept.
verses.arminianNotes: Esau runs, embraces, weeps. The mercy is genuine and personal—he is not a puppet. Reconciliation here is two brothers freely meeting; grace had been seeking this peace, and Esau does not refuse it.
verses.reformedNotes: The “but” is gospel-shaped: sword-fear meets a brother’s neck. God can turn a heart (cf. Prov 21:1) without making the tears fake. The God Jacob feared would send Esau as a hunter sends him as a weeper.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse a hollow hug. Arminians typically stress Esau’s real, uncoerced mercy and Jacob’s responsible approach; Reformed readers typically stress that God effectually turned the meeting from vengeance to tears without erasing either brother’s agency.

verses.text: And when Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and children, he said, “Who are these with you?” Jacob said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob names the children as gracious gift, and himself as “your servant.” Thanksgiving is honest: family is received, not seized. Grace-given offspring are confessed before the brother once cheated.
verses.reformedNotes: The first word over the household is God’s gracious giving. Offspring of promise appear not as Jacob’s trophy but as the Lord’s gift—providence already stocking the next generation in Canaan’s direction.

verses.text: Then the servants drew near, they and their children, and bowed down.
verses.arminianNotes: The first wave bows as instructed. Households can learn peace; even the least-protected come near instead of fleeing. Obedience in small companies is still a real act.
verses.reformedNotes: Servants and their children approach under the same mercy that met Jacob. God is settling a whole camp, not only a patriarch’s private fear.

verses.text: Leah likewise and her children drew near and bowed down. And last Joseph and Rachel drew near, and they bowed down.
verses.arminianNotes: Leah, then Rachel and Joseph: the whole family enacts humility. Peace is practiced in order, not only felt in Jacob’s chest. Each drawing-near is a grace-enabled step they actually take.
verses.reformedNotes: Joseph, last and dearest, still bows. The future savior of the family is already inside a story of lowered pride. God keeps the line while teaching the camp to bend.

verses.text: Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company that I met?” Jacob answered, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: The herds were a plea for favor. Jacob seeks Esau’s goodwill as a responsible peacemaker: gifts can serve reconciliation without buying it like a bribe if the heart is true.
verses.reformedNotes: “My lord” from the younger matches last night’s limp: God has been reducing Jacob. The company Esau met is means; the favor sought sits under the God who already granted life.

verses.text: But Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; keep what you have for yourself.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esau’s “I have enough, my brother” is real contentment and a real offer. He is not written as a foil only: he can refuse the gift without refusing the man. Kindness here is chosen.
verses.reformedNotes: “My brother” answers “my lord.” Providence has filled Esau’s hand too; he is not a leftover of the blessing. God can prosper the older without unseating the promise that runs through the younger.

verses.text: Jacob said, “No, please, if I have found favor in your sight, then accept my present from my hand. For I have seen your face, which is like seeing the face of God, and you have accepted me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jacob links Esau’s accepted face to seeing God’s face—Peniel still echoing. To receive a brother’s pardon is to taste mercy that could have been withheld. He pleads; he does not coerce.
verses.reformedNotes: The comparison is theological, not flattery only: the God whose face he saw at the Jabbok now shows that face in a brother’s welcome. Acceptance is gift twice over—divine and fraternal—under one Lord.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear Peniel in the brother’s face. Arminians typically stress a sincere, received pardon between two agents; Reformed readers typically stress that the God of the night vision effectually showed His favor through Esau’s acceptance.

verses.text: Please accept my blessing that is brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” Thus he urged him, and he took it.
verses.arminianNotes: He calls the gift a “blessing” and names God’s gracious dealing. Urging until Esau takes it is peacemaking completed: restored fellowship is sealed when the offended brother actually receives. Both remain free in the exchange.
verses.reformedNotes: The stolen blessing’s shadow meets an offered blessing. God has dealt graciously; Jacob now has “enough.” Providence writes surplus into the cheater’s hand so he can honor the brother without impoverishing the promise.

verses.text: Then Esau said, “Let us journey on our way, and I will go ahead of you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Esau offers escort and shared road. The invitation is brotherly and concrete. Jacob will have to answer it honestly; companionship can be received or declined.
verses.reformedNotes: The older offers to lead. God has turned threat into convoy—yet the promise’s map still runs toward Canaan, not merely toward Seir. Providence can use a kind offer without making it Jacob’s next obedience.

verses.text: But Jacob said to him, “My lord knows that the children are frail, and that the nursing flocks and herds are a care to me. If they are driven hard for one day, all the flocks will die.”
verses.arminianNotes: The care is real: frail children, nursing stock. Stewardship of the weak is a genuine reason. Whether caution also hides leftover fear, Jacob remains responsible for how he speaks and how he will travel.
verses.reformedNotes: Pace and tenderness are not unbelief by themselves. The God who gave the flocks also binds Jacob to them. Even so, the narrator will soon show a different destination than the one named.

verses.text: Let my lord pass on ahead of his servant, and I will lead on slowly, at the pace of the livestock that are ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
verses.arminianNotes: He promises Seir. Slow travel can be love for the little ones—or a polite distance. Scripture lets the tension stand: disciples still answer for words they do not keep.
verses.reformedNotes: “Until I come to my lord in Seir” is spoken; Canaan is where he will camp. God still shepherds the hesitant. The promise does not rest on Jacob’s travel itinerary being perfectly frank.

verses.text: So Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” But he said, “What need is there? Let me find favor in the sight of my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: A guard is offered and declined. Jacob seeks favor, not an armed escort. Preferring to go without Esau’s men is a real choice—prudence, independence, or leftover wariness; the text does not flatten him into a hero or a villain.
verses.reformedNotes: Esau’s people would have been a hedge. Jacob asks only favor. The Lord who kept him at the Jabbok will keep him without Esau’s four hundred; providence is enough cover.

verses.text: So Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
verses.arminianNotes: They part in peace the same day. Esau’s return is his own road, freely taken. Reconciliation does not require fusion of households; it required the embrace already given.
verses.reformedNotes: Seir receives Esau again. The older brother’s line has a place under God (later Edom) without inheriting Canaan. Providence separates roads without revoking the mercy of the neck and the kiss.

verses.text: But Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built himself a house and made booths for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth.
verses.arminianNotes: Not Seir: Succoth, a house, booths for stock. The detour is Jacob’s. Grace that reconciled him still leaves room for mixed motives—delay, safety, settlement. He remains accountable for the road he actually takes.
verses.reformedNotes: Succoth (“booths”) is east of the Jordan, not Esau’s mountain. God still brings him toward the land while the man builds sheds. Imperfect obedience does not cancel the Keep who named him Israel.
verses.keyContrast: Both notice he does not go to Seir. Arminians typically stress Jacob’s responsible, mixed choice to settle short; Reformed readers typically stress that God still advances him toward Canaan despite the unkept itinerary.

verses.text: And Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, on his way from Paddan-aram, and he camped before the city.
verses.arminianNotes: “Safely” (or peacefully) into Canaan: the vow’s country, not Laban’s. The pilgrim who feared Esau now camps as a sojourner. Safety is gift to be received with thanks, not presumed as a right.
verses.reformedNotes: From Paddan-aram to Shechem: the God of the going-out brings him in. “Safely” is the narrator’s verdict on providence. The land of promise holds his tent because the Lord said it would.

verses.text: And from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, he bought for a hundred pieces of money the piece of land on which he had pitched his tent.
verses.arminianNotes: He buys the plot—no raid, no claim by force. Peaceable purchase in Canaan is responsible sojourning: the promise is trusted without stealing a well or a field. Later grief at Shechem (ch. 34) does not rewrite this honest start.
verses.reformedNotes: A hundred qesitah, Hamor’s sons, a legal stake. Abraham bought a grave; Jacob buys a campsite. God lets the heir own a parcel inside the land He will one day give in full—earnest, not the whole inheritance.

verses.text: There he erected an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Altar and name: “God, the God of Israel.” The new name from the Jabbok becomes worship in Canaan. Calling on God is a free, fitting response to mercy received—the right first work after safe arrival.
verses.reformedNotes: El-Elohe-Israel confesses that the God of the fathers is now the God of this man newly named. Worship marks the land because God kept him. The altar is fruit of preserving grace, planted on purchased soil until a greater altar comes.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear covenant worship in the name. Arminians typically stress Jacob’s grateful, responsible confession after delivered mercy; Reformed readers typically stress that the God who named him Israel now publicly claims this man and this plot by His own keeping.
